prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enabled measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep B012 with Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. The case rests on the committee's own criterion, a discovery or invention, and not on the opening tally. The invention has a precise physical core: a magic wavelength at which the lattice light shift cancels, so that many neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and probed on an ultranarrow optical transition. The demonstrated result is fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, reproduced independently with Sr, Yb and Hg. Those are demonstrated results, not prospects. As an experimentalist I find reproduction across laboratories and species the most reliable evidence of maturity, and I give it more weight than any expected application. The chair's convergence note is right that eight members agreeing in round 1 is not evidence of merit. I therefore tested the case against the strongest objections raised and it still holds. The two-name credit also leaves room under the three-laureate limit, which avoids the arbitrary exclusions that members themselves describe for B039 and B029. I did not change my preferred configuration between round 1 and now. What changed is how I would defend it: I now rest it explicitly on demonstrated performance and independent reproduction, and I place the redefinition of the second and clock-based geodesy in the category of confirmation.
statement.case_against: The novelty margin over the 2005 prize (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks) is the real weakness, and seven members raise it, as the chair's summary records. I do not think it can be dismissed. My answer is that the earlier prizes honoured the comb as a tool and the control of individual ions, whereas the lattice clock resolves a different problem, namely how to combine the signal-to-noise of many atoms with freedom from motional and light-shift errors, and that is a separate invention. I accept that this is a judgment call. The other weakness is attribution. The roles of Katori and Ye, and the contributions of groups at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere, are known to the members mainly from recollection and not from verified records in our material. The pending redefinition of the second makes timing debatable, although not on scientific grounds. A prize this year is defensible, and a later one would be defensible too.

responses.point: The Higgs observation (B039) remains the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist, and the fact that it splits the committee over attribution should not be mistaken for a weaker scientific case; the clock has less dramatic discovery content.
responses.response: I agree that the scientific weight of B039 is not in dispute, and that attribution difficulty is not a reason to rank it lower on science. Where I part from you is on what the statutes ask of us. The prize is for a discovery or invention, and the committee has to name the people responsible for the original work. For B039 the leadership roles of Gianotti, Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee and the scientific authorship of a thousands-strong measurement are not separable inside three names, and your own round-1 text lists the Della Negra versus Virdee question among your open uncertainties. On discovery content I would say the lattice clock is an invention with a discovery attached: it opened a regime in which many-body and systematic-shift physics, and tests of constants, can now be done with an instrument that did not exist. If the committee wanted to pursue B039 I would want a written, verified account of the credit first. I cannot supply that, so I do not move it above B012.

responses.point: Waiting for the formal redefinition of the second is a defensible timing argument, and the step beyond combs and single-ion clocks may be judged incremental, since ion clocks, other lattice groups and later contributors such as Takamoto lie outside the two credited names.
responses.response: I have gone back and forth on the timing point and I come down against waiting. The redefinition is a decision by metrology bodies about a unit, and the physics case does not depend on it. If we made it a precondition we would be handing a scientific judgment to a procedural calendar. On Takamoto and the other groups, I accept your point that they matter, but the question is whether the original contribution is the concept plus the demonstration of the frontier performance, and on the record available to me that points to Katori and Ye. I would not add a third name to meet the objection, since I cannot verify the roles from the supplied material and a third name chosen from memory would be less defensible than two. You also described a possible field bias as a laser spectroscopist. I share the instinct to check for it, and as a microscopist I tested the opposite bias on myself in B021, which is why I do not advocate it.

responses.point: Part of the case rests on a pending application, and the question is whether lattice clocks and ion clocks should be treated as one field needing joint recognition or as a bounded invention.
responses.response: I would keep it as a bounded invention. Ion clocks sit on the control-of-single-quantum-systems line that was recognised in 2012, and the lattice clock is built on a different principle, many neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength trap. Joint recognition would force a longer list of names than the statutes allow and would blur the citation. The citation should therefore name the magic-wavelength trapping explicitly so that the boundary is written into the text. I agree with you that the pending application is part of the argument for some members, and I would not rely on it. If the committee judged the demonstrated performance alone insufficient, I would regard that as a reason to prefer a later year over a different candidate.

responses.point: If the committee prefers a prize tied to a new quantum phenomenon rather than a metrological instrument, B057 is the better answer, though its credit is incomplete without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
responses.response: I take B057 seriously, and I have moved it into my alternatives in place of B021 because of your argument and Mehlig's. My difficulty is the one you name: with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as the three credited names, the work of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, including the prediction in HgTe that Molenkamp's group then confirmed, would be left outside a three-name limit. That is a credit problem that the citation cannot repair, and it is a stronger obstacle than the novelty-margin objection to B012. So I agree that a new quantum phenomenon would be a different kind of result, but I do not think it is a better answer this year. If B012 did not obtain support, B057 or B036 would be where I would look next. I also note your disclosure on B051, which does not affect B012.

responses.point: There is a fair argument that a discovery in fundamental physics such as IceCube or the Higgs carries more weight with the wider community than a precision-metrology achievement, and the contributions of NIST, PTB, SYRTE and JILA colleagues make a two-name credit a simplification.
responses.response: The weight with the wider community is a reasonable consideration, but I would not let it override scientific judgment, and your own round-1 uncertainties raise the allocation among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA and Baikal pioneers as unresolved. I accept that a two-name credit is a simplification of a field effort. Every prize simplifies. The test I apply is whether the proposal and the demonstration of the frontier can be tied to named individuals, and for B012 they can, while for the collaboration-scale candidates the cap forces exclusions that the committee would struggle to justify. I do not want popularity to count as science. If the wider community's view is to enter at all, it should enter through the citation, which should say plainly what was invented and what level of performance was achieved.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the novelty margin over the 2005 and 2012 prizes sufficient. I believe it is, but I recognise it is a judgment call and not a measurable fact.

The priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and the relative roles of Katori, Ye and other groups. I rely on general knowledge, as several others do, and the supplied record does not let me verify it. The chair's first question should be answered with sources before the vote if possible.
How much weight to give prospective impact, including the redefinition of the second and clock-based geodesy, against demonstrated reproduction across laboratories.
Whether a two-name credit would still be judged complete if a later check showed that another group made a contribution as decisive as those of the credited pair.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I have no specific conflict with Katori, Ye or B012 from my profile, and my background in transmission electron microscopy is unrelated to optical clocks. My opening first choice, B021 (aberration-corrected electron optics), lies in my own field and my documented ties to the international microscopy community, so I would step back from deciding on it if it were advanced, and I have not listed it as an alternative this round. Göran Johansson is also at Chalmers. No credited name for B012, B036 or B057 is tied to Chalmers in my profile, and I have no unreported relationship to disclose. I note Johansson's disclosure on B051 and Eriksson's field proximity on B005 and B036, and I would support whatever ruling the chair makes on them.
